How the Phrase counts tab counts your phrases

The Phrase counts tab

You type a phrase. Sheets counts the rows that contain it, for each source.

Glassdoor

43 of 101 rows (42.6%)

YouTube

16 of 98 rows (16.3%)

Real counts from the class workbook. Type these same phrases in your workbook to check it's working.

The formula, in plain words

"Count the rows where source is glassdoor and text contains the phrase anywhere."

=COUNTIFS(Voice!$B$2:$B$200,"glassdoor",Voice!$C$2:$C$200,"*"&$A2&"*")

The * on each side means "anything before or after". That's why "pay" also counts "paying". The formulas are already in the tab. You only type phrases in A2 to A11.

Rows, not mentions

A row counts once, however many times it says the phrase.

  • One video chunk says “pay” five times. How much does it add to the YouTube count?

Percentages, not raw counts

Compare the % of each source's rows. It's fair for groups of any size.

Glassdoor has 101 rows and YouTube 98, so here the raw counts are close. With other data they often aren't.

  • Made up for practice: a phrase is in 10 of 101 Glassdoor rows and 10 of 50 YouTube rows. Which source mentions it more?

Read before you chart

Counts are a starting point. Ask three questions.

  1. In both sources? "break" is: 8 Glassdoor rows, 17 YouTube chunks.
  2. Leans to one? Glassdoor talks about pay far more. YouTube talks about managers far more.
  3. One speaker? "manager" passes: its 20 chunks come from 5 different videos.

  • “idle time” is in 5 YouTube chunks, all from one video. Pattern, or one worker's story?

Three things to remember

The tab does the counting. You do the reading.

  • Rows, not mentionsA row counts once, however often it says the phrase.
  • Compare %Use the share of each source's rows, not the raw count.
  • Check the speakerBefore you trust a YouTube count, see how many videos it comes from.
